entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4482"/><div sID="gen6493" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4482"/><hi type="bold">4. Skin for skin--</hi>a proverb. Supply, "He will give." The "skin" is figurative for any outward good. Nothing outward is so dear that a man will not exchange it for some other outward good; "but" (not "yea") "life," the inward good, cannot be replaced; a man will sacrifice everything else for its sake. Satan sneers bitterly at man's egotism and says that Job bears the loss of property and children because these are mere outward and exchangeable goods, but he will give up all things, even his religion, in order to save his life, if you touch his bones and flesh. "Skin" and "life" are in antithesis [Umbreit]. The martyrs prove Satan's sneer false. Rosenmuller explains it not so well. A man willingly gives up another's skin (life) for his own skin (life). So Job might bear the loss of his children, &c., with equanimity, so long as he remained unhurt himself; but when touched in his own person, he would renounce God. Thus the first "skin" means the other's skin, that is, body; the second "skin," one's own, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.21.28">Ex 21:28</reference>. <div eID="gen6493" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4484"/><div sID="gen6495" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4484"/><hi type="bold">7. sore boils--</hi>malignant boils; rather, as it is singular in the Hebrew, a "burning sore." Job was covered with one universal inflammation. The use of the potsherd [Job 2:8] agrees with this view. It was that form of leprosy called black (to distinguish it from the white), or elephantiasis, because the feet swell like those of the elephant. The Arabic judham (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.35">De 28:35</reference>), where "sore botch" is rather the black burning boil (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.6">Is 1:6</reference>). <div eID="gen6495" type="x-p"/>

Eliphaz--</hi>The view of Rawlinson that "the names of Job's three friends represent the Chaldean times, about 700 B.C.," cannot be accepted. Eliphaz is an Idumean name, Esau's oldest son (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.4">Ge 36:4</reference>); and Teman, son of Eliphaz (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.15">Ge 36:15</reference>), called "duke." Eusebius places Teman in Arabia-Petræa (but see on <reference osisRef="Job.6.19">Job 6:19</reference>). Teman means "at the right hand"; and then the south, namely, part of Idumea; capital of Edom (<reference osisRef="Amos.1.12">Am 1:12</reference>). Hebrew geographers faced the east, not the north as we do; hence with them "the right hand" was the south. Temanites were famed for wisdom (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.7">Jr 49:7</reference>). Baruch mentions them as "authors of fables" (namely, proverbs embodying the results of observation), and "searchers out of understanding."<div eID="gen6501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6502" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Bildad the Shuhite--</hi>Shuah ("a pit"), son of Abraham and Keturah (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.2">Ge 25:2</reference>). Ptolemy mentions the region Syccea, in Arabia-Deserta, east of Batanea.<div eID="gen6502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6503" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Zophar the Naamathite--</hi>not of the Naamans in Judah (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.41">Jos 15:41</reference>), which was too distant; but some region in Arabia-Deserta. Fretelius says there was a Naamath in Uz. <div eID="gen6503" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4490"/><div sID="gen6505" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4490"/><hi type="bold">13. seven days ... nights--</hi>They did not remain in the same posture and without food, &c., all this time, but for most of this period daily and nightly. Sitting on the earth marked mourning (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.10">La 2:10</reference>). Seven days was the usual length of it (<reference osisRef="Gen.50.10">Ge 50:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.13">1Sa 31:13</reference>). This silence may have been due to a rising suspicion of evil in Job; but chiefly because it is only ordinary griefs that find vent in language; extraordinary griefs are too great for utterance. <chapter eID="Job.2"/>
